title: More women reach the top, but workplace equality promises outpace action
subtitle: A new ILO report finds gains in business leadership alongside weaker implementation of measures that support women’s careers. Its survey exposes a gap between commitments and practice.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Employers increasingly say gender equality helps their businesses. Yet the practical measures that can help women stay in work and advance are reaching fewer firms in the International Labour Organization’s latest survey comparison.

The ILO’s Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success, released on 3 November, reports that almost three quarters of responding enterprises had an equality and diversity policy or equivalent in 2025. Across the initiatives examined, however, the average proportion reporting implementation was 26.5 per cent, down from 37.4 per cent in 2018.

That gap matters to women assessing a job, seeking promotion or returning after childbirth. A policy can establish a commitment. It cannot, by itself, demonstrate that pay decisions are fair, that leave is usable or that complaints are handled safely.
Progress at the top, uncertainty below

The report finds gains in women’s representation in senior leadership, alongside weaker gender balance at junior and middle management levels. Women still hold less than a third of managerial positions worldwide, according to the ILO’s separate modelled labour-market estimates.

The findings complicate a familiar measure of progress: counting women at the summit. More women leading businesses is significant. But a company’s most visible appointment does not reveal whether women elsewhere in the organisation have comparable access to the experience, responsibilities and promotions that lead there.

Among the measures losing ground in the survey comparison were maternity leave and support programmes and equal-pay initiatives. At the UN’s Geneva briefing on 3 November, the ILO identified these, along with measures against harassment, as areas employers themselves considered effective.

For workers, the relevant questions are concrete. Who qualifies for support? Who uses it? What happens to their pay and progression afterwards? Those questions turn a broad promise into something employees and their representatives can scrutinise.
What the evidence can—and cannot—show

The 2025 enterprise survey collected responses from 11,957 businesses across 99 countries between June and September last year. It used a global enterprise panel and distribution through employer and business membership organisations.

These are findings about participating enterprises, not statistically representative estimates of every business worldwide. The samples also changed between survey rounds. The figures therefore do not establish that the same companies withdrew support, or identify a single political or commercial cause for the decline.
The implementation figure is an average across different measures. It should not be read as saying that only 26.5 per cent of businesses did anything at all to advance equality.

Nearly seven in ten surveyed enterprises reported that equality and diversity initiatives improved business outcomes, the ILO says. These are employers’ assessments. They do not, on their own, prove that a particular initiative caused higher profits, or that appointing a woman to lead a company automatically improves its performance.

ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo called for commitments to become measurable progress. His argument combines a business incentive with a rights obligation: equality should not depend on a woman first proving that fair treatment increases an employer’s earnings.
Making a future visible

One case study in the report offers a practical example. At Philippine logistics company Airspeed, the ILO describes recruitment, promotion and pay processes organised around explicit performance criteria. The company began tracking its gender initiatives through indicators and a scorecard in 2025, including women’s representation in hiring, promotions and leadership.
“And when women know they have a future in the company, they shine,” founder and chairperson Rosemarie P. Rafael told the report’s authors.

The account is a selected company case study, not an independent experiment or a guarantee that its approach transfers unchanged to every workplace. Its useful lesson is the emphasis on observable decisions: who is recruited, who progresses and how results are monitored.

The report leaves employers with a more demanding test than publishing a policy or celebrating a senior appointment. They need to show whether the route to advancement is becoming accessible throughout the organisation.

For women considering their next move, that means looking beyond the promise of opportunity to the evidence of it. A credible future at work should be visible in the people who progress, the support they can use and the accountability when commitments are not met.
The Athena Perspective.
